name: Apple Scab
summary: A common fungal disease of apple that causes dark, scabby spots on leaves and fruit. Severe infections cause early leaf drop and unmarketable, cracked fruit.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown, velvety spots on the upper leaf surface that later turn black
Leaves become curled, yellow and drop early
Dark, corky, scab-like lesions on fruit that may crack
Young infected fruit can become misshapen
conditions: Cool, wet spring weather. Leaves that stay wet for 9 hours or more at 15-24 °C allow infection. The fungus survives the winter in fallen leaves.

cultural: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves to remove the source of spring infection
Prune the canopy to improve air flow and speed up drying
Spray 5% urea on fallen leaves after harvest to speed up their decomposition
organic: Wettable sulphur 80 WP @ 2 g/L as a protective spray (avoid above 30 °C)
Bacillus subtilis based bio-fungicide as per label
chemical: Hexaconazole 5 EC @ 0.5 ml/L or Difenoconazole 25 EC @ 0.3 ml/L (curative, rotate groups)

fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen in spring; soft new growth is more susceptible
Maintain adequate potassium and calcium for strong leaf and fruit tissue
prevention: Plant scab-resistant varieties where available
Begin protective sprays from green-tip stage during wet weather
Do not leave infected leaves and fruit in the orchard

name: Apple Black Rot
summary: A fungal disease that attacks leaves, fruit and branches. On leaves it causes 'frog-eye' spots; on fruit it causes a firm brown rot that ends in black, shrivelled mummies.
symptoms: Small purple spots on leaves that enlarge into brown 'frog-eye' spots with a purple margin
Brown rot on fruit, often starting at the blossom end, with concentric rings
Rotted fruit turns black and shrivels into a mummy
Sunken, reddish-brown cankers on branches
conditions: Warm, wet and humid weather (about 20-32 °C). Spores spread from mummified fruit, dead wood and cankers, and enter through wounds.

cultural: Remove mummified fruit from trees and the ground
Prune out dead wood and cankered branches, cutting well below the canker
Burn or bury removed material away from the orchard
organic: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L at the dormant stage
chemical: Thiophanate-methyl 70 WP @ 1 g/L (rotate with the above)

fertilizer: Keep trees vigorous with balanced NPK based on soil test; stressed trees are more prone to cankers
Avoid late-season nitrogen that delays hardening of wood
prevention: Avoid wounding fruit and bark
Control insects that create entry wounds
Maintain orchard sanitation every season

name: Cedar Apple Rust
summary: A rust disease that needs two hosts to complete its life cycle: apple and juniper (cedar). It causes bright orange spots on apple leaves and fruit.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface
Small black dots in the centre of the spots
Tube-like structures on the underside of the leaf below the spots
Raised orange lesions on fruit
conditions: Wet spring weather at 13-24 °C. Spores are released from galls on nearby juniper or cedar trees. The disease is uncommon where junipers are absent.

cultural: Remove juniper or cedar trees, or their galls, near the orchard where practical
Remove heavily infected leaves
organic: Wettable sulphur 80 WP @ 2 g/L as a protective spray
chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 3 g/L from pink-bud to petal-fall

fertilizer: Use balanced nutrition; there is no specific nutrient cure for rust
Avoid heavy nitrogen in spring
prevention: Choose rust-resistant apple varieties
Apply protective sprays during wet weather in spring

name: Healthy Apple
summary: No visible disease was detected on this apple leaf. Keep monitoring the orchard, especially during wet spring weather when scab and rust spread.
fertilizer: Apply fertilizer according to tree age and soil or leaf analysis
Supply nitrogen in split doses before flowering and after fruit set
prevention: Inspect leaves weekly for spots or powdery growth
Keep the orchard floor clean of fallen leaves and fruit
Prune annually for good light and air movement

name: Healthy Blueberry
summary: No visible disease was detected on this blueberry leaf. Blueberries need acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.5); yellowing leaves often indicate high soil pH rather than disease.
fertilizer: Use ammonium-based nitrogen (for example ammonium sulphate); blueberries do not use nitrate well
Keep soil pH at 4.5-5.5; add elemental sulphur if pH is too high
prevention: Mulch with pine bark or sawdust to keep roots cool and moist
Prune old canes to keep bushes open

name: Cherry Powdery Mildew
summary: A fungal disease that forms a white, powdery coating on young leaves and fruit. It weakens the tree and lowers fruit quality.
symptoms: White, powdery patches on leaves, mostly on young growth
Leaves curl upward and become distorted
White fungal growth or russeting on fruit
conditions: Warm days, cool nights and high humidity at 15-27 °C. Unlike most fungi, it does not need free water on the leaf. Dense canopies favour it.

cultural: Prune to open the canopy and improve air flow
Remove root suckers and water sprouts, which are often infected first
organic: Wettable sulphur 80 WP @ 2 g/L (do not spray above 32 °C)
Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3-5 ml/L
Potassium bicarbonate sprays as per label

fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen; lush growth is highly susceptible
Ensure adequate potassium
prevention: Begin monitoring at shoot growth in spring
Keep tree canopies open
Avoid planting in shaded, poorly ventilated sites

name: Healthy Cherry
summary: No visible disease was detected on this cherry leaf. Continue routine monitoring for powdery mildew and leaf spot during humid weather.
fertilizer: Apply nitrogen in early spring according to tree age
Use leaf analysis every 2-3 years to guide fertilizer
prevention: Prune for an open canopy
Inspect young shoots weekly for white powdery growth

model_label: Corn (Maize) with Cercospora and Gray Leaf Spot
name: Maize Gray Leaf Spot
summary: A fungal leaf disease of maize that produces long, grey, rectangular lesions. Heavy infection before grain fill can cause large yield losses.
symptoms: Small tan spots with a yellow halo on lower leaves
Spots become long, narrow, rectangular grey-to-tan lesions limited by leaf veins
Lesions join together and kill large areas of the leaf
conditions: Warm (25-30 °C) and very humid weather with long periods of dew or fog. Common in continuous maize with crop residue left on the surface.

cultural: Rotate with a non-host crop (such as pulses) for at least one season
Plough in or remove infected crop residue after harvest
organic: Trichoderma-based seed and soil treatment as per label to reduce early infection
chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L at first symptoms

fertilizer: Apply balanced N and K; potassium deficiency increases disease severity
Do not delay the nitrogen top dressing, as stressed plants suffer more
prevention: Grow tolerant or resistant hybrids
Avoid continuous maize in the same field
Scout lower leaves from knee-high stage onward

name: Maize Common Rust
summary: A rust disease that forms small, powdery, cinnamon-brown pustules on both sides of maize leaves. Severe early infection reduces grain filling.
symptoms: Small, oval, cinnamon-brown powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules release rust-coloured powder when rubbed
Pustules turn dark brown to black late in the season
Heavily infected leaves yellow and dry
conditions: Cool to moderate temperatures (16-25 °C) with high humidity and at least 6 hours of dew. Spores are carried long distances by wind.

cultural: Remove and destroy heavily infected lower leaves in small plots
Destroy volunteer maize plants
organic: Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3-5 ml/L may slow early spread
chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L at first appearance of pustules

fertilizer: Use balanced nutrition; excess nitrogen can increase rust severity
Maintain adequate potassium
prevention: Grow rust-resistant hybrids
Sow at the recommended time to avoid cool, humid periods at the susceptible stage

name: Maize Northern Leaf Blight (Turcicum)
summary: A fungal disease that causes long, cigar-shaped grey-green lesions on maize leaves. Infection before silking can cut yield significantly.
symptoms: Long (2.5-15 cm) elliptical, cigar-shaped grey-green lesions
Lesions turn tan as they mature
Symptoms start on lower leaves and move upward
Dark spore growth on lesions in humid weather
conditions: Moderate temperatures (18-27 °C) with heavy dew, frequent rain and high humidity. The fungus survives in infected crop residue.

cultural: Rotate crops and manage residue by ploughing it in
Remove severely infected lower leaves in small plots
organic: Trichoderma harzianum-based products as a soil and residue treatment
chemical: Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole premix as per label

fertilizer: Apply recommended N and K in splits; nutrient stress increases blight
Correct zinc deficiency, which is common in maize
prevention: Grow resistant hybrids
Avoid dense planting that keeps leaves wet
Scout fields regularly before tasselling

name: Healthy Maize
summary: No visible disease was detected on this maize leaf. Keep scouting lower leaves weekly, since leaf blights and rust start there.
fertilizer: Apply nitrogen in splits: at sowing, knee-high stage and pre-tasselling
Apply zinc sulphate (25 kg/ha) on zinc-deficient soils
prevention: Rotate maize with pulses or oilseeds
Scout for fall armyworm and leaf diseases weekly

name: Grape Black Rot
summary: A fungal disease that causes brown leaf spots and turns berries into hard, black, shrivelled mummies. It can destroy most of the crop in wet seasons.
symptoms: Circular tan-to-brown leaf spots with a dark border
Tiny black dots (fruiting bodies) inside the spots
Berries turn brown, then shrivel into hard black mummies
Black lesions on shoots and tendrils
conditions: Warm, wet weather (20-30 °C) with rain splash. The fungus survives in mummified berries and infected canes.

cultural: Remove all mummified berries from vines and the ground
Prune out infected canes during winter pruning
Manage the canopy so bunches dry quickly
organic: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L as a protective spray

fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen that produces a dense, humid canopy
Ensure adequate potassium for berry development
prevention: Start protective sprays from early shoot growth in wet seasons
Keep the vineyard free of mummies and debris

name: Grape Esca (Black Measles)
pathogen: Fungal complex (Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium spp. and others)
summary: A wood disease caused by several fungi that enter through pruning wounds. It produces 'tiger-stripe' leaf patterns and spotted berries, and can kill vines. There is no curative spray.
symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' pattern: yellow or red-brown bands between leaf veins
Small dark spots on berries (measles)
Dark streaks in the wood when the trunk is cut
Sudden wilting and collapse of the vine in hot weather
conditions: Infection enters through large pruning wounds, especially when pruning in rainy weather. Symptoms show up more in hot summers and on water-stressed vines.

cultural: Cut out and burn infected wood well below the visible streaking
Retrain a new trunk from a healthy shoot where possible
Prune in dry weather and avoid large pruning cuts
organic: Protect fresh pruning wounds with a Trichoderma-based wound paste
chemical: No effective curative fungicide exists; seal large pruning wounds with a fungicide-based wound paint as per label

fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition and avoid water stress, which makes symptoms worse
prevention: Prune late in the dormant season during dry weather
Disinfect pruning tools between vines
Use certified healthy planting material

name: Grape Leaf Blight (Isariopsis Leaf Spot)
summary: A fungal leaf spot disease that causes dark brown, irregular spots and early leaf fall. Loss of leaves weakens the vine and reduces fruit quality.
symptoms: Irregular dark-brown to red-brown spots on leaves, often with a yellow margin
Dark fungal growth on the underside of spots
Spots join together and leaves dry and drop early
conditions: Warm and humid weather (22-32 °C), especially late in the season. Spreads from infected fallen leaves.

cultural: Collect and destroy fallen infected leaves
Thin the canopy to improve air movement
organic: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L

fertilizer: Use balanced nutrition; maintain potassium and magnesium levels
prevention: Keep vineyard floor clean
Avoid overhead irrigation that wets leaves

name: Healthy Grape
summary: No visible disease was detected on this grape leaf. Downy and powdery mildew are the main risks in humid weather, so keep monitoring.
fertilizer: Apply fertilizer in splits after back pruning and fruit pruning, based on petiole analysis
Potassium is important from berry set to ripening
prevention: Check the underside of leaves for downy growth after rain
Maintain an open canopy

name: Citrus Greening (Huanglongbing)
pathogen: Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, spread by the Asian citrus psyllid
summary: One of the most destructive citrus diseases. It is caused by a bacterium carried by the citrus psyllid insect. There is no cure; infected trees decline and produce small, bitter fruit.
symptoms: Blotchy, uneven yellow mottling across leaf veins (not symmetrical)
Yellow shoots and small, upright leaves
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stays green at the bottom end
Twig dieback and overall tree decline
conditions: Spread by the Asian citrus psyllid, which multiplies on new leaf flushes in warm weather (25-30 °C), and by infected budwood.

cultural: Remove and destroy confirmed infected trees to protect healthy ones
Plant only certified disease-free nursery plants
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor psyllids
organic: Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3-5 ml/L on new flushes to deter psyllids
chemical: Imidacloprid 17.8 SL @ 0.3 ml/L during new flush (psyllid control)

fertilizer: Foliar micronutrient sprays (zinc sulphate 0.5%, manganese, magnesium) may help infected trees stay productive longer
Maintain balanced NPK and good root health
prevention: Control psyllids on every new flush
Inspect trees regularly and remove suspect trees quickly
Never use budwood from unknown sources

name: Peach Bacterial Spot
summary: A bacterial disease that causes small angular spots and 'shot holes' on leaves and pitting or cracking on fruit. It spreads with wind-driven rain.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked angular spots on leaves that turn purple-brown
Spot centres fall out, giving a 'shot-hole' look
Leaves yellow and drop early
Small dark pits and cracks on fruit
conditions: Warm (24-30 °C), wet and windy weather. Worse on sandy soils and stressed trees.

cultural: Prune out infected twigs during dry weather
Plant windbreaks to reduce wind-driven rain
Avoid overhead irrigation
organic: Copper hydroxide 77 WP @ 2 g/L at leaf fall and bud swell (copper can injure peach leaves in season; use low rates)
chemical: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L during dormancy
Do not use antibiotic sprays: streptomycin and tetracycline are banned for agricultural use in India

fertilizer: Keep trees vigorous with balanced fertilizer; weak trees suffer more
Avoid excessive nitrogen
prevention: Grow less susceptible varieties
Maintain good tree vigour and drainage

name: Healthy Peach
summary: No visible disease was detected on this peach leaf. Keep watching for leaf curl in spring and bacterial spot in wet weather.
fertilizer: Apply nitrogen in early spring and after harvest, based on tree age
Use leaf analysis to fine-tune fertilizer
prevention: Prune for an open-centre canopy
Apply a dormant copper spray in areas with leaf curl history

name: Bell Pepper Bacterial Spot
summary: A seed-borne bacterial disease that causes leaf spots, leaf drop and scabby spots on fruit. It spreads quickly in warm, rainy weather.
symptoms: Small water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown with a yellow halo
Heavy leaf drop, exposing fruit to sunscald
Raised, scabby, brown spots on fruit
conditions: Warm (24-30 °C), wet weather, rain splash and overhead irrigation. Carried on seed and crop debris.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected plants and debris
Do not work in the field when plants are wet
Switch from overhead to drip irrigation
organic: Bacillus subtilis based bio-bactericide as per label
Copper hydroxide 77 WP @ 2 g/L
chemical: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L every 7-10 days in wet weather
Copper oxychloride + Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2 g/L tank mix improves control
Do not use antibiotic sprays: streptomycin and tetracycline are banned for agricultural use in India

fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen
Supply calcium and potassium for strong tissue
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed or hot-water treated seed (50 °C for 25 minutes)
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2-3 years
Use drip irrigation

name: Healthy Bell Pepper
summary: No visible disease was detected on this bell pepper leaf. Keep monitoring for bacterial spot in rainy weather and for mites and thrips in dry weather.
fertilizer: Apply nitrogen in splits; increase potassium from flowering onward
Calcium supply and even watering prevent blossom-end rot
prevention: Use drip irrigation and mulch
Inspect undersides of leaves weekly

name: Potato Early Blight
summary: A fungal disease that causes dark, ring-patterned 'target' spots on older leaves. It reduces leaf area and tuber yield, and is worse on stressed or poorly fed plants.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings ('target board') on older, lower leaves
Yellow tissue around the spots
Spots join and leaves dry and drop
Dark, sunken, dry lesions on tubers
conditions: Warm temperatures (20-30 °C) with alternating wet and dry periods. Plants under nutrient or water stress and older crops are more affected.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves
Destroy crop debris after harvest
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2-3 years
organic: Trichoderma viride or Bacillus subtilis based bio-fungicide as per label
Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3-5 ml/L as a supporting spray
chemical: Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/L or Difenoconazole 25 EC @ 0.5 ml/L (rotate groups)

fertilizer: Do not let the crop run short of nitrogen and potassium; nutrient stress increases early blight
Apply the remaining nitrogen at earthing up
prevention: Use healthy, certified seed tubers
Keep plants well watered and fed
Start preventive sprays when the first spots appear on lower leaves

name: Potato Late Blight
summary: The most destructive potato disease. In cool, humid weather it can destroy an entire field within a week. It also rots tubers in the field and in storage. Act immediately.
symptoms: Pale or dark-green water-soaked patches on leaf tips and edges
Patches quickly turn brown-black
White, downy growth on the leaf underside in humid mornings
Dark lesions on stems; reddish-brown dry rot inside tubers
conditions: Cool, humid weather: 10-25 °C with relative humidity above 90% for 10 hours or more, cloudy days, fog or drizzle.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately; do not leave them in the field
Earth up (hill) the rows to protect tubers
Cut and remove haulms 10-15 days before harvest in infected fields
organic: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L as a protective spray
chemical: Before disease: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L as a preventive spray when weather is favourable
After disease appears: Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 3 g/L
Or Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L, or Dimethomorph 50 WP @ 1 g/L (rotate; repeat after 7-10 days)

fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen, which produces dense, humid foliage
Ensure adequate potassium for tuber quality
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers
Destroy cull piles and volunteer potato plants
Follow local late blight forecasts and spray preventively when cool, humid weather is expected

name: Healthy Potato
summary: No visible disease was detected on this potato leaf. Watch closely for late blight whenever the weather turns cool, cloudy and humid.
fertilizer: Apply half the nitrogen and all phosphorus and potassium at planting; the rest at earthing up
Potato responds well to potassium
prevention: Use certified seed tubers
Earth up rows properly
Scout fields twice a week in cool, humid weather

name: Healthy Raspberry
summary: No visible disease was detected on this raspberry leaf. Good air movement and removal of old canes keep cane diseases low.
fertilizer: Apply nitrogen in early spring
Mulch with compost to keep roots moist
prevention: Remove fruited canes after harvest
Keep rows narrow for good air flow

name: Healthy Soybean
summary: No visible disease was detected on this soybean leaf. Monitor for rust, yellow mosaic and leaf-eating caterpillars during the monsoon season.
fertilizer: Treat seed with Rhizobium and PSB culture; soybean fixes most of its own nitrogen
Apply sulphur (20-30 kg/ha) on deficient soils
prevention: Ensure good drainage; soybean does not tolerate waterlogging
Remove plants showing yellow mosaic early

name: Squash Powdery Mildew
summary: A very common fungal disease of squash and other cucurbits. White powder covers the leaves, causing early leaf death and smaller, poorer-quality fruit.
symptoms: White, powdery spots on both sides of leaves
Spots spread until leaves are covered
Leaves turn yellow, then brown and die early
Fruits ripen early and have poor flavour
conditions: Warm temperatures (20-30 °C), high humidity, shade and dense planting. It does not need rain or free water on leaves.

cultural: Remove the worst affected older leaves
Space plants for sunlight and air movement
organic: Wettable sulphur 80 WP @ 2 g/L (avoid hot days; some cucurbit varieties are sulphur-sensitive)
Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3-5 ml/L
Potassium bicarbonate sprays as per label

fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen
Maintain balanced potassium
prevention: Grow resistant varieties
Start sprays at the first spots; early control is much easier

name: Strawberry Leaf Scorch
summary: A fungal disease that covers strawberry leaves with small purple spots until they look burnt or scorched. It weakens plants and lowers yield in the next season.
symptoms: Many small, irregular purple spots on the upper leaf surface
Spot centres stay dark (no white centre, unlike leaf spot)
Spots join and the leaf dries out, looking scorched
Lesions may also appear on stalks and flower parts
conditions: Warm, wet weather (20-30 °C) with rain splash. The fungus survives on old infected leaves.

cultural: Remove and destroy old infected leaves
Renovate beds after harvest
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers
organic: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 2 g/L as a protective spray

fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen, which keeps the canopy dense and wet
Maintain adequate potassium
prevention: Plant resistant varieties and disease-free runners
Keep good spacing between plants
Mulch to reduce splash

name: Healthy Strawberry
summary: No visible disease was detected on this strawberry leaf. Keep leaves dry and remove old foliage to prevent leaf scorch and leaf spot.
fertilizer: Use fertigation with balanced NPK in small, frequent doses
Increase potassium during fruiting
prevention: Use drip irrigation and plastic or straw mulch
Remove runners and old leaves regularly

name: Tomato Bacterial Spot
pathogen: Xanthomonas spp. (X. vesicatoria, X. perforans and others)
summary: A seed-borne bacterial disease that causes many small dark spots on leaves and scabby spots on fruit. It spreads quickly in warm, rainy weather.
symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves, often with a yellow halo
Spots dry and the leaf looks ragged; leaves yellow and drop
Small raised, scabby spots on green fruit
conditions: Warm (24-30 °C), wet weather, rain splash and overhead irrigation. The bacteria survive on seed, debris and volunteer plants.

cultural: Remove and destroy badly infected plants and debris
Do not handle plants when they are wet
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead irrigation
organic: Bacillus subtilis based bio-bactericide as per label
Copper hydroxide 77 WP @ 2 g/L
chemical: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L every 7-10 days in wet weather
Copper oxychloride + Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2 g/L tank mix improves control
Do not use antibiotic sprays: streptomycin and tetracycline are banned for agricultural use in India

fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen
Supply calcium and potassium for strong tissue
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and healthy transplants
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2-3 years
Stake plants to keep leaves off the soil

name: Tomato Early Blight
summary: A common fungal disease that creates dark, ring-patterned spots on older tomato leaves. It causes leaf drop from the bottom up and can also rot fruit at the stem end.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings ('target board') on older leaves
Yellowing around the spots
Leaves die and drop from the bottom of the plant upward
Dark, leathery, sunken spots near the fruit stem
conditions: Warm (20-30 °C), humid weather with heavy dew. Spores splash up from infected soil and debris. Stressed, heavily fruiting plants are more affected.

cultural: Remove infected lower leaves and destroy them
Mulch the soil to stop spores splashing onto leaves
Stake or cage plants for better air flow
organic: Trichoderma viride or Bacillus subtilis based bio-fungicide as per label
Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3-5 ml/L as a supporting spray
chemical: Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/L or Difenoconazole 25 EC @ 0.5 ml/L (rotate groups)

fertilizer: Keep nitrogen and potassium adequate during fruiting; hungry plants get more blight
Avoid heavy single doses of nitrogen
prevention: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2-3 years
Use healthy transplants
Water at the base of the plant, not on leaves

name: Tomato Late Blight
summary: A fast-spreading and destructive disease. In cool, humid weather it can kill plants and rot fruit within days. Act immediately.
symptoms: Large, irregular, greasy grey-green patches on leaves that turn brown-black
White downy growth on the leaf underside in humid conditions
Dark brown lesions on stems
Firm, greasy brown blotches on green fruit
conditions: Cool, humid weather: 10-25 °C with relative humidity above 90%, cloudy days, fog or drizzle. Spores spread quickly with wind and rain.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected plants and fruit immediately
Do not compost infected material
Improve spacing and avoid wetting leaves
organic: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L as a protective spray
chemical: Before disease: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L as a preventive spray when weather is favourable
After disease appears: Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 3 g/L
Or Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L, or Dimethomorph 50 WP @ 1 g/L (rotate; repeat after 7-10 days)

fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen
Ensure adequate potassium and calcium
prevention: Do not plant tomato near potato fields with blight
Spray preventively when cool, humid weather is forecast
Use tolerant varieties where available

name: Tomato Leaf Mold
summary: A fungal disease mostly seen in polyhouses and humid, poorly ventilated fields. It causes yellow patches on top of leaves and olive-green mould underneath.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow patches on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to greyish-purple velvety mould on the underside
Leaves curl, wither and drop
conditions: Very high humidity (above 85%) and moderate temperatures (20-26 °C), typical of closed polyhouses and dense plantings.

cultural: Improve ventilation and reduce humidity in polyhouses
Remove lower and infected leaves
Avoid wetting leaves while irrigating
organic: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L
Bacillus subtilis based bio-fungicide as per label

fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen that creates dense foliage
Maintain balanced potassium
prevention: Grow resistant varieties
Keep wider plant spacing and prune for air flow
Ventilate polyhouses in the morning

name: Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot
summary: A fungal disease that covers lower tomato leaves with many small spots with grey centres. Heavy leaf loss exposes fruit to sunscald and lowers yield.
symptoms: Many small, round spots (2-3 mm) with dark brown edges and grey-tan centres
Tiny black dots in the centre of the spots
Starts on lower leaves; leaves yellow and drop from the bottom up
conditions: Warm (20-27 °C), wet, humid weather with rain splash. The fungus survives on crop debris and weeds of the tomato family.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves
Mulch to prevent soil splash
Control weeds such as nightshade
organic: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L

fertilizer: Keep plants well fed with balanced NPK
Avoid heavy nitrogen alone
prevention: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2 years
Stake plants and use drip irrigation
Clean up all debris after harvest

model_label: Tomato with Spider Mites or Two-spotted Spider Mite
name: Tomato Two-spotted Spider Mite
summary: Tiny mites feed on the underside of leaves, causing fine yellow speckling, bronzing and webbing. Populations explode in hot, dry weather.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white speckles (stippling) on leaves
Leaves turn bronze, dry out and drop
Fine silk webbing on the underside of leaves and between stems
Tiny moving dots visible with a hand lens
conditions: Hot, dry weather (27-38 °C) with low humidity, dusty conditions and water-stressed plants. Overuse of broad-spectrum insecticides kills natural predators and causes outbreaks.

cultural: Remove and destroy heavily infested leaves
Spray water on the underside of leaves to dislodge mites and raise humidity
Avoid water stress in the crop
organic: Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3-5 ml/L, covering the leaf underside
Wettable sulphur 80 WP @ 2 g/L (avoid above 32 °C)
Release or conserve predatory mites where available
chemical: Use a miticide (acaricide), not a general insecticide
Fenazaquin 10 EC @ 2 ml/L or Abamectin 1.9 EC @ 0.5 ml/L (rotate; mites develop resistance fast)

fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen, which increases mite reproduction
Keep plants irrigated; drought-stressed plants suffer more
prevention: Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticide sprays
Control weeds that host mites
Check leaf undersides weekly in hot, dry weather

name: Tomato Target Spot
summary: A fungal disease that produces brown spots with concentric rings on leaves, stems and fruit. Severe attacks cause heavy leaf drop.
symptoms: Small brown water-soaked spots that grow into round lesions with rings and a light centre
Lesion centres may crack
Sunken brown spots on fruit
Leaves yellow and drop
conditions: Warm (20-30 °C), humid weather with long periods of leaf wetness.

cultural: Remove infected leaves and crop debris
Improve air flow by pruning and staking
Avoid overhead irrigation
organic: Bacillus subtilis based bio-fungicide as per label
chemical: Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/L or Difenoconazole 25 EC @ 0.5 ml/L (rotate groups)

fertilizer: Use balanced NPK; avoid excess nitrogen
prevention: Rotate crops and destroy debris
Keep leaves dry

name: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV)
pathogen: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (Begomovirus), spread by whitefly Bemisia tabaci
summary: A viral disease spread by whiteflies. Infected plants become stunted with small, curled, yellow leaves and set very little fruit. There is no cure, so control focuses on whiteflies and removing infected plants.
symptoms: Leaves curl upward and become cup-shaped
Yellowing of leaf edges and between veins
Small leaves, stunted and bushy plants
Flower drop and very poor fruit set
conditions: Hot, dry weather (25-35 °C) when whitefly populations are high. Infection of young plants causes the greatest loss.

cultural: Uproot and destroy infected plants early to stop spread
Install yellow sticky traps (10-15 per acre) to monitor and trap whiteflies
Remove weeds that host whiteflies
organic: Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3-5 ml/L to deter whiteflies
Grow 2-3 border rows of maize or sorghum as a barrier crop
chemical: The virus cannot be cured; sprays target the whitefly vector
Imidacloprid 17.8 SL @ 0.3 ml/L or Thiamethoxam 25 WG @ 0.3 g/L
Spiromesifen 22.9 SC @ 1 ml/L or Diafenthiuron 50 WP @ 1 g/L (rotate groups)

fertilizer: Balanced nutrition helps plants tolerate infection but will not cure it
Avoid excess nitrogen, which attracts whiteflies
prevention: Grow TYLCV-resistant or tolerant hybrids
Raise seedlings under 40-50 mesh insect-proof net
Use silver reflective mulch to repel whiteflies

name: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV)
summary: A very stable virus that spreads through contact: hands, tools, clothing and seed. It causes mottled light and dark green leaves and poor-quality fruit. There is no cure.
symptoms: Light and dark green mosaic or mottled pattern on leaves
Leaves become distorted, narrow or fern-like
Stunted plants
Uneven ripening and internal browning of fruit
conditions: Spreads mechanically through handling, pruning, tools and infected seed. Not strongly weather-dependent. The virus survives for a long time in plant debris.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected plants, handling them last
Wash hands with soap and water before touching healthy plants
Disinfect tools in 10% household bleach or 3% trisodium phosphate
organic: Dipping hands in milk while working can reduce spread
chemical: No chemical cures viral diseases; focus on hygiene and resistant varieties

fertilizer: Balanced nutrition only; there is no nutrient cure
prevention: Use certified, treated seed and resistant varieties
Do not use tobacco products while handling plants
Remove crop debris after harvest

name: Healthy Tomato
summary: No visible disease was detected on this tomato leaf. Keep monitoring for blights in humid weather and for whiteflies and mites in hot, dry weather.
fertilizer: Apply phosphorus and potassium at planting and nitrogen in 2-3 splits
Keep soil moisture even to prevent blossom-end rot
prevention: Stake plants and remove lower leaves touching the soil
Use drip irrigation and mulch
Inspect plants twice a week
